q: Does the SIMULATeQCD HIP back end deliver a portable performance ceiling on AMD MI250X (Frontier) and MI300X, and how does an equivalent SYCL / Intel-oneAPI path (needed for Aurora PVC) compare, on a per-kernel basis, to the CUDA path on Frontier-era A100/H100 vs Perlmutter A100?
basis: Paper Sec 5.2 (via REPORT.md §4.9, C4, C12) claims tri-back-end support (cuda / hip_nvidia / hip_amd) and reports MI250X HISQ Dslash numbers 1.63→ 40.63 TFLOP/s (strong) and 0.93→165.72 TFLOP/s (weak) at 1→256 GCDs on Frontier, and the authors themselves candidly note 'single-GPU MI250X performance lags what single-A100 memory bandwidth would predict' and 'we are investigating what is causing this decreased performance'. Our replication verified only the CUDA path on 8×A100 sm_80 (uicgpu) and only via CMake configure for the hip_amd branch on macOS — no MI250X/MI300X execution, and no SYCL/oneAPI back end exists at all despite Aurora being an active exascale target for lattice QCD.
next_steps: (1) Obtain OLCF Frontier / ALCF Aurora / LLNL El Capitan / ORNL early-access allocations; rebuild SIMULATeQCD with BACKEND=hip_amd on MI250X + MI300X and re-run confReadWriteTest, compressionTest, plus the HISQ Dslash micro-benchmark at 1/8/64/256 GCDs; (2) prototype a SYCL/oneAPI back end (or DPC++ port) targeting Intel PVC, validate correctness against the CUDA baseline on the 20^4 β=6.498 plaquette test, and produce a per-kernel roofline for Dslash, gauge update, and gradient flow on all three vendors; (3) publish a cross-vendor kernel-performance-ceiling table (achieved TFLOP/s vs peak memory bandwidth vs peak flop rate) so the community can see where each back end sits relative to hardware limits, not just relative to each other.

q: What are the true multi-GPU strong- and weak-scaling limits of SIMULATeQCD's HMC on exascale systems (Frontier, Aurora, El Capitan) for both staggered (HISQ) and Wilson fermions, and how do those limits compare against the CPU-era Milc and Chroma benchmarks that dominated lattice-QCD scaling reports through the 2010s?
basis: REPORT.md Table in §4.9 reports Perlmutter 96^4 strong-scale 5.07→96.47 TFLOP/s and Frontier 96^4 strong-scale 1.63→40.63 TFLOP/s for HISQ Dslash only — not for a full HMC trajectory, and only up to 256 GPUs/GCDs, an order of magnitude below full-machine scale on Frontier (~37k GCDs) or Aurora. No Wilson-fermion scaling data is reported. No comparison to the historical Milc/Chroma CPU baselines is provided, making it hard for the community to know whether SIMULATeQCD's scaling floor is set by algorithmic parallelism, communication, or vendor-runtime overhead.
next_steps: (1) Run a full HISQ+2+1-flavor RHMC trajectory (not just Dslash) at 512/1024/2048/4096/8192/16384 GPU counts on Perlmutter and Frontier, measuring MDU/wall-hour and communication vs compute breakdown; (2) exercise the (currently under-supported) Wilson-fermion path with an analogous scaling sweep; (3) publish head-to-head plots of RHMC MDU/wall-hour and communication overhead for SIMULATeQCD vs Chroma vs MILC on the same problem sizes; (4) identify the communication primitive (halo exchange, all-reduce in the CG solver, GPU-GPU peer copies) that first saturates and file back-end optimization tickets against it.

q: What is the physics impact of running the HISQ Dslash and its inverter in reduced precision (FP16, BF16, TF32, FP8) vs the FP64/FP32 mixed-precision baseline that HotQCD ensembles were generated with, specifically on the observables that matter (chiral susceptibility, topological charge, Polyakov-loop susceptibility, screening masses, Taylor coefficients)?
basis: SIMULATeQCD ships four SU(3) link-compression schemes (R18/R14/R12/U3R14, verified in REPORT.md §4.6/§5.1 with the 20^4 β=6.498 compressionTest → plaquette 0.6382 matching NERSC header 0.6381995717 to displayed precision), but this only tests the storage round-trip. The framework's actual solvers, Dslash kernel, and gauge-update paths were not exercised in reduced precision, and there is no published study of how FP16/BF16/TF32/FP8 propagate into physical observables. Modern Hopper/Blackwell hardware exposes FP8 tensor cores that could dramatically accelerate the solver but only if physics observables tolerate the reduction.
next_steps: (1) Implement (or verify existence of) FP16/BF16/TF32/FP8 solver + Dirac-operator variants; (2) generate matched short HISQ ensembles at a fixed β in each precision mode and measure chiral susceptibility, topological charge, Polyakov susceptibility, screening masses, and Taylor coefficients; (3) compute observable deltas vs the FP64/FP32 baseline and publish a precision-vs-observable-bias table so that ensemble-generation campaigns can pick the coarsest precision that leaves physics untouched; (4) provide a fallback mechanism that automatically escalates precision on solver convergence failure.

q: Can SIMULATeQCD's HMC autocorrelation time (especially for topological charge at fine lattice spacings) be reduced by an order of magnitude by integrating machine-learning-accelerated proposal generation (normalizing flows, diffusion-based samplers) alongside the framework's existing Symanzik-improved-action + gradient-flow noise-reduction toolchain?
basis: REPORT.md §1 confirms the framework already ships Symanzik-improved actions, gradient flow, HYP smearing, and multilevel updates as first-class physics modules (Sec 3 of the paper). But autocorrelation time for topological charge τ_Q at fine a explodes towards continuum — the well-known 'freezing' problem — and none of the shipped noise-reduction techniques solve it. The lattice-QCD community has demonstrated in the last few years (e.g., normalizing-flow samplers, ML-assisted HMC) that ML-generated proposals can partially unfreeze topology, but SIMULATeQCD ships no such integration.
next_steps: (1) Prototype a PyTorch/JAX normalizing-flow proposal generator that emits SU(3) gauge configurations, wire it into SIMULATeQCD's RHMC accept/reject stage as an alternative proposal move; (2) measure integrated autocorrelation time τ_int for Q_top, plaquette, and chiral condensate on matched short ensembles with and without the ML proposal at a=0.06, 0.045, 0.03 fm; (3) evaluate at least one diffusion-based sampler as a second ML approach; (4) publish speedup-in-effective-samples per wall-hour vs pure HMC, honestly reporting where ML helps and where it does not; (5) ensure the ML component is optional and does not become a required dependency of the core framework.

q: What sustainable-software-engineering plan (CI/CD, container-based reproducibility, automated performance regression testing, cross-machine tuning-database curation) would let SIMULATeQCD survive as a decade-scale community lattice-QCD codebase across three or more hardware generations, and does that plan need to be built into the framework itself or maintained separately by the HotQCD collaboration?
basis: REPORT.md §4.1 documents 230 C++ files / 62,619 lines under src/ with active post-publication development (new applications checkConf, measureHadrons, sampleTopology; new top-level dirs examples/, experimental/, tools/). REPORT.md §4.8 also shows how easily a build breaks in an unusual environment (macOS CLT stdlib gap for the HIP path). The paper does not commit to a container image, does not describe a public CI matrix covering CUDA + HIP + (future) SYCL, and does not describe a performance-regression harness that would catch a 20% throughput regression on the next CUDA-runtime upgrade. Without such infrastructure, a 62k-line HPC codebase risks bit-rot across the exascale transition.
next_steps: (1) Publish a versioned container (Apptainer/Singularity + Docker) per release tag that pins CUDA / ROCm / MPI / compiler versions and passes the full shipped test suite; (2) stand up a public CI matrix (GitHub Actions self-hosted runners against small A100 / MI250X boxes) that builds all three back ends on every PR and runs confReadWriteTest, compressionTest, and a short HISQ Dslash micro-bench; (3) build an automated performance-regression harness that runs the Dslash micro-bench nightly and alerts on >10% throughput regression vs a baseline commit; (4) publish and curate a cross-machine tuning database (block sizes, comm strategies, precision defaults per hardware SKU) so users on new machines start with tuned defaults instead of framework defaults; (5) formalize a code-ownership + review policy at HotQCD so the framework survives PI turnover across the decade.
